module_title: Azure Data Factory and Synapse Pipelines
title: ADF architecture, integration runtimes and linked services
summary:
ADF architecture, integration runtimes and linked services is an engineering capability within azure data factory and synapse
pipelines.
content:
ADF architecture, integration runtimes and linked services is an engineering capability within azure data factory and synapse
pipelines. In a production platform, it is not just a tool or a one-off transformation: it is a repeatable design decision that affects
correctness, scalability, security, operability and the experience of downstream data consumers.
The central design question is how to achieve the required outcome while controlling service selection, secure configuration,
data movement, operational monitoring and cost-aware deployment. Engineers should make assumptions explicit: what is the
source of truth, what constitutes a valid record, how is progress tracked, what happens when work is repeated, and how can
the system recover after interruption?
A robust implementation separates configuration from processing logic, uses stable identifiers and explicit contracts, and
records enough metadata to explain what ran, which input it processed, what it produced and whether the output passed
validation. The correct design depends on workload size, concurrency, latency, retention, compliance, team capability and the
cost of failure.
For adf architecture, integration runtimes and linked services, distinguish the logical pattern from the product implementation.
Products change, but the underlying principles—clear contracts, deterministic processing, bounded resource use,
observability, least privilege and tested recovery—remain applicable across platforms.

REAL-WORLD INDUSTRY EXAMPLE
A company operates sales, ERP and web-activity systems across business units. It uses Azure services to implement adf
architecture, integration runtimes and linked services, landing source data in governed storage and publishing trusted
analytical datasets to reporting and operational consumers.

PRACTICAL IMPLEMENTATION AND DESIGN GUIDANCE
1. Begin with the business SLA, data classification, source connectivity, expected volume, latency, recovery and cost
envelope.
2. Select the Azure service based on service selection, secure configuration, data movement, operational monitoring and
cost-aware deployment. Avoid choosing a service solely because it is familiar.
3. Use managed identity wherever supported, least-privilege RBAC/ACLs, Key Vault for secrets and private connectivity for
sensitive paths.
4. Implement the flow with the relevant components from Azure Data Factory, ADLS Gen2, Azure Databricks, Synapse
Analytics, Event Hubs, Azure Monitor and Microsoft Entra ID. Parameterize environments and keep configuration separate
from code.
5. Capture pipeline/job run metadata, diagnostic logs, data-quality results, freshness and volume metrics.
6. Validate retries, duplicate delivery, partial failures, replay, deployment rollback and budget alerts in a non-production
environment.

IMPORTANT POINTS TO REMEMBER
• State the business and technical problem that adf architecture, integration runtimes and linked services solves.
• Explain the main design trade-offs around service selection, secure configuration, data movement, operational monitoring and cost-aware
deployment.
• Make processing repeatable and safe under retries and partial failure.
• Validate outputs with explicit quality, freshness and completeness checks.
• Measure reliability, performance and cost rather than relying on assumptions.

title: Triggers, schedules and event-based orchestration
summary:
Triggers, schedules and event-based orchestration is an engineering capability within azure data factory and synapse
pipelines.
content:
Triggers, schedules and event-based orchestration is an engineering capability within azure data factory and synapse
pipelines. In a production platform, it is not just a tool or a one-off transformation: it is a repeatable design decision that affects
correctness, scalability, security, operability and the experience of downstream data consumers.
The central design question is how to achieve the required outcome while controlling event contracts, partition keys, time
semantics, state and replay. Engineers should make assumptions explicit: what is the source of truth, what constitutes a valid
record, how is progress tracked, what happens when work is repeated, and how can the system recover after interruption?
A robust implementation separates configuration from processing logic, uses stable identifiers and explicit contracts, and
records enough metadata to explain what ran, which input it processed, what it produced and whether the output passed
validation. The correct design depends on workload size, concurrency, latency, retention, compliance, team capability and the
cost of failure.
For triggers, schedules and event-based orchestration, distinguish the logical pattern from the product implementation.
Products change, but the underlying principles—clear contracts, deterministic processing, bounded resource use,
observability, least privilege and tested recovery—remain applicable across platforms.

REAL-WORLD INDUSTRY EXAMPLE
A company operates sales, ERP and web-activity systems across business units. It uses Azure services to implement triggers,
schedules and event-based orchestration, landing source data in governed storage and publishing trusted analytical datasets
to reporting and operational consumers.

PRACTICAL IMPLEMENTATION AND DESIGN GUIDANCE
1. Begin with the business SLA, data classification, source connectivity, expected volume, latency, recovery and cost
envelope.
2. Select the Azure service based on event contracts, partition keys, time semantics, state and replay. Avoid choosing a
service solely because it is familiar.
3. Use managed identity wherever supported, least-privilege RBAC/ACLs, Key Vault for secrets and private connectivity for
sensitive paths.
4. Implement the flow with the relevant components from Azure Data Factory, ADLS Gen2, Azure Databricks, Synapse
Analytics, Event Hubs, Azure Monitor and Microsoft Entra ID. Parameterize environments and keep configuration separate
from code.
5. Capture pipeline/job run metadata, diagnostic logs, data-quality results, freshness and volume metrics.
6. Validate retries, duplicate delivery, partial failures, replay, deployment rollback and budget alerts in a non-production
environment.

IMPORTANT POINTS TO REMEMBER
• State the business and technical problem that triggers, schedules and event-based orchestration solves.
• Explain the main design trade-offs around event contracts, partition keys, time semantics, state and replay.
• Make processing repeatable and safe under retries and partial failure.
• Validate outputs with explicit quality, freshness and completeness checks.
• Measure reliability, performance and cost rather than relying on assumptions.
